explanation: No shared concept: fires on a wide mix of tokens (Japanese particles and commas, mid-word subword pieces in Russian/English such as 'ож', 'Glob', 'ucle', 'it', code punctuation, numbers, ordinary function words) across languages and domains, with no consistent lexical or contextual trigger.

Mostly fires on a content word or function word that completes a familiar multiword expression or collocation, e.g. 'RNA [polymer]ase', 'no choice [but]', 'get [away] with', 'under the [cover] of', 'fundamental [rights]', 'Brilliant [Green]'. Strength depends on the preceding words predicting this continuation, but the pattern is loose and many examples fit only weakly.

Fires on tokens in generic boilerplate or marketing/web-copy prose: strongest on 'WITHOUT' in the Apache license line '"AS IS" BASIS, WITHOUT WARRANTIES', and moderately on function words and sentence-ending periods in SEO-style promotional text ('They [can] be easily modified', 'needs[.] We offer'). Little response in technical or narrative text.

Fires on pieces of acronyms and abbreviations or institution names, especially the second or later part of a capitalized abbreviation (Check [Point], B[PO], C[PO], Ch[M], EM[R], HP[SE], M[.D]), and also on a sentence-initial 'With' at the start of a news paragraph. Weak elsewhere.

Fires on the opening tokens of code-file header boilerplate: the ' *' on the first line after '/**' in PHP/Java/JS files, 'Copyright' in an AssemblyCopyright attribute, 'localhost' or '/TR' in URLs. It also fires separately on the contraction "'s" in a sentence-initial "That's" and on 'Lumpur' after 'Kuala'.

Fires on a mid-word subword fragment that follows a short initial piece like 'st'/'St'/'mon'/'Mon' inside a longer word or name, most of all on 'arch' (St-arch, Mon-arch, dist-arch, mon-arch) and 'ax' in DataSt-ax, with weaker hits on other second fragments ('ak', 'unt', 'ang', 'ases'). The token's position as a word-internal continuation is what matters.

Fires on scattered tokens with no clear common thread: foreign-language word fragments (Malay 'sambil', Tagalog 'Dapat', German 'Flughafen', Portuguese 'tortura'), repeated list headings like 'CHAPTER', code/XML tokens, place names and numbers. Activations are mostly moderate.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word at a hyphen or word start, especially chemical-nomenclature pieces like '-n' in 'p-nitroanilide', 'N-normetaz', 'III-nitride', '-V' in 'Rappaport-Vassiliadis', and on the first piece of proper names that get split into several tokens (Nippur, Dibrugarh, Penobscot, Münster) or of words like 'nifedipine' and 'nucleotides'. The trigger is the start of a word the tokenizer splits up, often one that starts with 'n'.

Fires on the first subword piece 'le'/'Le'/'LE', 'al'/'Al' or 'med'/'Med' at the start of a word that continues into more pieces (le-ptic, -le-ader, le-athery, le-ptin, al-derman, al-veolus, Eid al-, Med-iation, med-ulla, Le-ukotriene, LE-HMAN). The token must start a longer word; standalone uses are weak.

Fires on the first token of a new clause or sentence in opinionated, emotional or narrative prose: periods and semicolons that end a clause, and the following pronoun, determiner or connective ('; [the] pain', 'Frustration[.]', '[It] wasn't', 'you [can]'). It does this most in persuasive or personal writing, weakly elsewhere.

Fires on words for physical or abstract connection: 'coupled'/'coupling' (mechanical, chemical, physical, as in 'inductively coupled plasma') and 'joint'/'Joint' (anatomical joints, 'Joint Committee', 'Joint Venture'). It responds moderately to related words like 'league', 'ligands', 'clutch' and 'couples'.

Fires on a mixture of tokens: subword pieces of all-caps datelines (SANTA CL[ARA], ANCH[ORAGE], J[ACK]SON, PETERSBUR[G]), digits in date/time stamps ('+0[0]00', 'August [2]'), a newline closing a Go struct body, and assorted function words. There is no single trigger.

Fires on a mix of tokens, often the second piece of a split word or identifier in code or legal/citation boilerplate (BOOST_SPIR[IT], PER CURI[AM], MS[Build], j[frog]) and digits inside DOI or article IDs (ijerph-[1]7, JAHA.[1]17), along with ordinary prose words. There is no consistent concept.

Fires mostly on structural tokens in code and structured text: assignment ' =' in 'x = true', '::' scope operators, path separators, identifier pieces after a namespace (FastJSON[Result], BoCA::[Config]), digits in citation IDs ('[@B1-ijerph-17-0[1]'), and the comma after the weekday in an email 'Sent: Monday, ...' header. Weak in ordinary prose.
